summary: Defines terminology for discussing network mobility (NEMO), where a whole network moves and changes its attachment point to the Internet. The terms are meant to be used consistently in the NEMO issues and solution requirements. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a whole bus full of devices drives around, it needs words to describe its parts. This note sets the vocabulary so everyone means the same thing.

subtitle: The shared vocabulary for talking about a whole network that moves and changes its attachment to the Internet.

tldr.problem: When a router carrying a whole network changes its point of attachment, sessions between nodes in that network and the Internet break, and people need exact words to discuss it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terms for the components, node roles, nesting, multihoming, home network models and kinds of mobility support.
tldr.outcome: It is a terminology document with no protocol and no security considerations. Its NEMO Basic Support definition points at RFC 3963.

today: RFC 4885 is an Informational RFC from July 2007 and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. The solution it names for NEMO Basic Support is RFC 3963.

sections.title: What Network Mobility Is
sections.content:
Network mobility support is about managing the mobility of an entire network. It arises when the router connecting a network to the Internet changes its point of attachment, so reachability of the whole network changes. Such a network is a mobile network. Without support, sessions between its nodes and the global Internet cannot survive the move.

The RFC notes that NEMO can mean either a NEtwork that is MObile (a noun, as in "a NEMO") or NEtwork MObility (the concept, as in "NEMO Basic Support", and the working group's name). The terms are meant to be consistent with the IPv6 terminology, with RFC 3753 and with Mobile IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: If a train carries a whole classroom of computers, the train's router has to stay connected to the Internet for everyone. NEMO is the name for that problem.

sections.title: Architectural Components
sections.content:
A mobile network is one or more mobile IP subnets viewed as a single unit, connected by one or more mobile routers (MRs). An MR has egress interfaces facing the home or foreign link, and ingress interfaces facing links inside the mobile network. Upstream packets leave through an egress interface to the access router (AR); downstream packets enter through an ingress interface.

  • Mobile Network Prefix (MNP): the leading bits of an address that identify the whole mobile network; all nodes in it have an address with this prefix.
  • Mobile Network Node (MNN): any host or router inside the mobile network, permanently or temporarily.
  • Correspondent Node (CN): any node communicating with one or more MNNs.
  • Correspondent Router (CR) and Correspondent Entity (CE): used for route optimization sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: The mobile router is the front door of the moving network. Doors facing outward go to the world, doors facing inward go to the devices inside.

sections.title: Node Roles and Nested Mobility
sections.content:
Mobile network nodes come in three functional kinds:

  • Local Fixed Node (LFN): belongs to the mobile network and cannot change its attachment point while keeping sessions.
  • Local Mobile Node (LMN): a mobile node or router whose home link belongs to the mobile network.
  • Visiting Mobile Node (VMN): a mobile node or router whose home link is not part of the mobile network, currently attached to it.

Nested mobility is when a mobile network lets visiting nodes or whole networks attach, for example passengers on a bus using the bus's public access network. A sub-NEMO attached to a parent-NEMO forms a nested mobile network whose top is the root-NEMO, reached through the root-MR. Depth counts the sub-MRs a packet crosses between an MNN and the root-MR, and a node in the root-NEMO is at depth 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Some devices live on the bus, some are visitors. And a passenger can carry a mini network of their own, which then rides on the bus network like a boat on a bigger boat.

sections.title: Multihoming Terms
sections.content:
A host or MNN is multihomed when it has several addresses to choose between, because it is multi-prefixed (several prefixes advertised on its link) or multi-interfaced (several interfaces to choose from). The same logic gives a multihomed mobile router, and a multihomed mobile network exists when an MR is multihomed or there are multiple MRs to choose between.

A nested mobile network is multihomed when a root-MR is multihomed or there are several root-MRs. A split-NEMO is when a mobile network becomes two or more independent networks because the MRs handling the same MNP are separated. The RFC works through two scenarios of NEMO-1 and NEMO-2 attaching to each other to show which becomes parent, sub or root.
sections.plainLanguage: Having more than one way out to the Internet, like a house with two roads, is called multihoming. This section names the different ways a moving network can have that.

sections.title: Home Network Model Terms
sections.content:
These terms describe how mobile networks are configured at home. In Mobile IPv6 a home address derives from the home network prefix. In NEMO a home address can come from the home network or from one of the mobile router's MNPs.

  • Mobile Home Network: a mobile network that is also a home network.
  • Distributed Home Network: a home network spread geographically between sites, with the aggregated home prefix partitioned between them.
  • Mobile Aggregated Prefix: an aggregation of MNPs.
  • Aggregated Home Network, Extended Home Network and Virtual Home Network: variants built on aggregated prefixes; the Extended one is an aggregation that is further subnetted.
sections.plainLanguage: A home network is where a device officially lives. These words say what kinds of homes a moving network can have, including homes that are spread out or that themselves move.

sections.title: Mobility Support Terms
sections.content:
Host Mobility Support keeps sessions going when a mobile host changes attachment, via Mobile IPv6 or other mechanisms. Network Mobility Support does the same when a mobile router changes attachment, and is split into two classes.

  • NEMO Basic Support: bidirectional tunneling between MRs and their home agents (HAs), like Mobile IPv6 without route optimization. Only the HA and MR are NEMO-enabled, and RFC 3963 is the specified solution.
  • NEMO Extended Support: performance optimizations, including route optimization between arbitrary MNNs and CNs.

The MRHA tunnel is the bidirectional tunnel between an MR and its HA. A pinball route is the indirect path packets take when routed through one or more home agents, bouncing off them like a ball.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic way is to send all traffic through a helper back home, which works but takes the long way around. The extended way tries shortcuts.
